source.title: How to Talk So Kids Will Listen & Listen So Kids Will Talk
source.attribution: Summary in our own words of How to Talk So Kids Will Listen & Listen So Kids Will Talk by Adele Faber and Elaine Mazlish (1980). Not affiliated with or endorsed by the authors or publisher.
source.notes: Original summary written by Reborn; contains no text from the book. The book is in copyright. Skill lists checked against the book's chapter structure (helping children deal with feelings, engaging cooperation, alternatives to punishment, encouraging autonomy, praise, freeing children from playing roles).

cards.title: How children feel drives how they behave
cards.body:
Faber and Mazlish build the whole book on one link: when children feel understood, they tend to behave better, and when their feelings are brushed aside, behaviour gets worse. A child told "you're not tired" or "there's nothing to be scared of" learns that their own inner signals can't be trusted, and often gets more upset.

The authors suggest starting with the feeling rather than the behaviour. Acknowledging what a child feels is often the quickest way to calm things down.
cards.apply_it: Listen for the next time you say 'You don't really feel that'. Try naming the feeling instead.

quiz.question: What do Faber and Mazlish say happens when children's feelings are denied?
options: They often become more upset and confused
quiz.explanation: Dismissing feelings tends to escalate upset rather than calm it.

cards.title: Give a troubled child your full attention
cards.body:
The first skill the authors teach for helping with feelings is simple and often skipped: stop what you're doing and really listen. Half-listening while scrolling or cooking tells a child their trouble isn't worth your time, and they may stop trying to tell you.

Full attention, with eye contact and an open face, can be enough on its own. Sometimes a child just needs a sympathetic listener, not a solution.
cards.apply_it: Next time your child starts telling you something important, put down what you're holding and turn towards them.

quiz.question: What is the first skill the book suggests for helping a child with difficult feelings?
options: Asking why they feel that way
quiz.explanation: Simply attending fully often helps a child more than any words.

cards.title: Small sounds like 'Oh' or 'Mmm' can help a child think
cards.body:
Faber and Mazlish observe that parents often rush in with questions, advice or reassurance when a child is upset. Instead they suggest acknowledging with a brief word or sound: "Oh," "Mmm," "I see."

These small responses show you're with them without taking over. Given that space, children often talk their way through the problem and arrive at their own solution, which they're far more likely to follow than one you hand them.
cards.apply_it: In your next conversation with an upset child, hold back advice and just respond with short acknowledgements for two minutes.

quiz.question: Why do the authors recommend brief acknowledgements like 'Mmm'?
options: They are a polite way to ignore the child
They show you're listening and leave room for the child to find solutions
They replace the need for limits
quiz.explanation: Brief acknowledgements keep you present while letting the child think it through.

cards.title: Put a name to your child's feeling
cards.body:
Another skill from the book is to name the feeling you think the child is having: "That sounds really frustrating," or "You seem disappointed." Parents sometimes worry this will make the feeling stronger. Faber and Mazlish found the opposite: children are usually comforted when someone puts words to what they're going through.

Naming feelings also gives children a vocabulary for their inner world, which helps them understand and manage emotions as they grow.
cards.apply_it: Next time your child is upset, try one sentence that names the feeling, like 'You sound really disappointed.'

quiz.question: What do the authors say usually happens when a parent names a child's feeling?
options: The child is comforted that someone understands
The child stops talking to the parent
quiz.explanation: Hearing their feeling named usually comforts children.

cards.title: Give in fantasy what you can't give in reality
cards.body:
When a child wants something you can't provide, explaining logically why not often just fuels the argument. Faber and Mazlish suggest a playful alternative: grant the wish in imagination. "I wish I could make the rain stop right now. I wish I had a magic wand to make the cereal box full again."

The answer hasn't changed, but the child feels understood. Hearing their longing taken seriously can make the disappointment easier to bear.
cards.apply_it: Next time you have to say no, add a wish: 'I wish I could...' and see how your child responds.

quiz.question: What does 'granting wishes in fantasy' mean in the book?
options: Telling the child to stop wishing
Voicing the wish imaginatively while keeping your answer
quiz.explanation: You acknowledge the longing playfully without changing the limit.

cards.title: Accept all feelings, but limit harmful actions
cards.body:
A key distinction in the book: every feeling is allowed, but not every action. A child may be furious with a sibling, and that anger deserves to be heard. Hitting the sibling is still not allowed.

Faber and Mazlish suggest acknowledging the feeling and stating the limit together: you can see how angry they are, and people are not for hurting, so they can tell you or draw it instead. Children learn that emotions are normal and that they can choose what to do with them.
cards.apply_it: Practise one sentence that does both: 'You're really angry with your brother. I won't let you hit. Tell me with words.'

quiz.question: What distinction do the authors make about feelings and actions?
options: All feelings and all actions are acceptable
All feelings are acceptable, but some actions must be limited
quiz.explanation: Feelings are always allowed; harmful behaviour still has limits.

cards.title: Skip the 'why' questions when your child is upset
cards.body:
Faber and Mazlish note that asking an upset child "Why do you feel that way?" or "Why did you do that?" often backfires. Children frequently don't know why, or the question sounds like an accusation that demands a defence.

Instead of interrogating, the authors suggest reflecting what you see and hear. Statements often open a child up where questions shut them down.
cards.apply_it: Replace one 'Why did you...?' today with a statement such as 'Something about school seems to be bothering you.'

quiz.question: Why do the authors caution against 'why' questions with upset children?
options: They are too difficult to spell
Children often don't know why, and it can feel like an accusation
quiz.explanation: 'Why' can feel like a demand to justify, which shuts children down.

cards.title: Hold back advice, philosophy and pity when your child is hurting
cards.body:
The book lists familiar responses that rarely help an upset child: denying the feeling, giving a mini-lecture about life, offering quick advice, analysing their motives, defending the other person, or pitying them. Each, however well meant, tells the child their experience isn't really being heard.

Faber and Mazlish invite parents to imagine being on the receiving end. When you're upset, you want understanding first. Advice lands better later, if at all.
cards.apply_it: Recall a time someone gave you advice when you just wanted to be heard. Let that memory guide your next response to your child.

quiz.question: Which of these does the book list as an unhelpful response to an upset child?
quiz.explanation: Quick advice, like lectures or pity, skips over the child's feelings.

cards.title: Describe the problem instead of blaming the child
cards.body:
To get cooperation, Faber and Mazlish suggest describing what you see rather than attacking. "There's a wet towel on the bed" invites a child to fix it. "You always leave your things everywhere" invites them to defend themselves.

When you describe the problem, the child can work out what needs doing. Blame, insults and accusations usually make children feel attacked, and attacked people rarely want to help.
cards.apply_it: Notice your next instruction to your child. Rephrase it as a simple description of what you see.

quiz.question: According to the book, why does describing the problem work better than blaming?
options: It lets the child work out what to do without feeling attacked
It means the parent can avoid the issue
Children prefer to be told off
quiz.explanation: Description invites action; blame triggers defence.

cards.title: Give information, not orders
cards.body:
Rather than a command, the book suggests offering a piece of useful information: "Milk goes sour when it's left out." "Wet coats belong on the hook." Information is a gift a child can use for life, and it carries an assumption that they'll do the right thing once they know.

Faber and Mazlish point out that commands invite resistance, while information treats children as capable people who can act on what they learn.
cards.apply_it: Turn one daily command into information, for example 'Teeth get cavities if they aren't brushed at night.'

quiz.question: What do the authors suggest giving children instead of orders?
quiz.explanation: Information respects the child's ability to choose the right action.

cards.title: Say it in one word
cards.body:
Children tune out long speeches. Faber and Mazlish suggest that once the child already knows what's expected, a single word is often enough: "Pyjamas." "The dog." "Shoes."

A one-word reminder is short, free of lecturing and leaves the child to fill in the rest themselves. It saves your breath and spares both of you the familiar nagging spiral.
cards.apply_it: Pick one repeated reminder in your house and replace it with a single word for a week.

quiz.question: When do the authors suggest using a one-word reminder?
options: When the child doesn't know the rule
When the child already knows what's expected
quiz.explanation: A one-word cue works when the child knows the expectation and just needs a prompt.

cards.title: Tell children how you feel, without attacking them
cards.body:
Parents have feelings too, and the book encourages expressing them honestly. The trick is to talk about yourself rather than about the child's character: "I don't like being pulled at," not "You're so annoying."

Faber and Mazlish argue that children can respond to a parent's genuine feelings when they aren't being insulted at the same time. Honest feelings without attacks teach children that other people's needs matter.
cards.apply_it: Next time you're irritated, start your sentence with 'I feel' or 'I don't like' and describe the action, not the child.

quiz.question: How do the authors suggest parents express their own frustration?
options: Talk about their own feelings without attacking the child
quiz.explanation: Honest 'I' statements give information without insult.

cards.title: Write a note when talking isn't working
cards.body:
Faber and Mazlish suggest a surprisingly effective tool: a written note. A note on the fridge or the bathroom door can say what spoken nagging cannot, without the tone of voice that sets off resistance. It can be playful, even written as if from the object itself, and it lasts longer than a passing remark.

For children who can't read yet, a simple drawing can work. For teenagers, a brief text can do the same job.
cards.apply_it: Write a short, light-hearted note about one recurring problem and leave it where the problem happens.

quiz.question: Why can a written note work when spoken reminders fail?
options: It avoids tone of voice and can be playful
It allows parents to avoid their children
Children are legally required to follow notes
quiz.explanation: Notes remove nagging tones and can add humour.

cards.title: Drop threats, sarcasm, lectures and comparisons
cards.body:
The book lists common ways parents try to get cooperation that tend to backfire: blaming, name-calling, threats, commands, lecturing, warnings, martyrdom ("after all I've done for you"), comparisons with siblings, sarcasm and gloomy predictions about the child's future.

Faber and Mazlish invite parents to imagine hearing these themselves. Most produce resentment, guilt or a sense of worthlessness, not willing cooperation.
cards.apply_it: For one day, keep a tally of threats, sarcasm and comparisons you use. Just noticing is the first step.

quiz.question: Which of these does the book list as a habit that undermines cooperation?
options: Comparing a child with their sibling
quiz.explanation: Comparisons, like threats and sarcasm, breed resentment rather than cooperation.

cards.title: Punishment can leave children thinking about revenge, not repair
cards.body:
Faber and Mazlish question whether punishment teaches what parents hope. They observe that children who are punished often focus on how unfair it was or on getting back at the parent, rather than on what they did and how to put it right.

The authors don't suggest letting everything go. They offer a set of alternatives that hold children responsible while keeping the relationship intact and helping the child learn.
cards.apply_it: Think about the last time your child was punished. What did they seem to learn: the lesson, or resentment?

quiz.question: What concern do the authors raise about punishment?
options: It can distract children from taking responsibility
It is the only effective approach
quiz.explanation: Punishment can shift a child's focus to unfairness or revenge instead of amends.

cards.title: Show strong disapproval without attacking character
cards.body:
Among the alternatives to punishment, the book suggests stating your disapproval clearly and with feeling, but about the action, not the child: "I'm very upset that the new saw was left out in the rain."

Then state your expectation: tools come back after use. Faber and Mazlish argue that this lets children know exactly what was wrong and what you expect, without leaving them feeling they are bad people.
cards.apply_it: Next time something goes wrong, say what upset you and what you expect from now on, in two sentences.

quiz.question: What two things do the authors suggest parents state instead of punishing?
options: Their disapproval of the action and their expectation
Their disappointment in the child's character
quiz.explanation: Strong feeling about the action plus a clear expectation teaches without shaming.

cards.title: Show children how to make amends
cards.body:
Rather than punishing, Faber and Mazlish suggest showing a child how to put things right. If a toy is broken, help them think how to fix or replace it. If someone is hurt, ask what they could do to help.

Making amends teaches children that mistakes can be repaired and that they have the power to do so. Children learn responsibility by acting on it, not by suffering for it.
cards.apply_it: Next time your child causes a problem, ask: 'What can you do to make this right?' and help them follow through.

quiz.question: What do the authors suggest children learn from making amends?
options: That mistakes can be repaired by their own actions
quiz.explanation: Making amends gives children a way to take responsibility.

cards.title: Offer a choice between two acceptable options
cards.body:
When a child keeps misbehaving, the book suggests offering a choice: "You can walk next to the trolley, or sit in it. You decide." Both options are fine with you, and the child gets some control.

Faber and Mazlish explain that choices give children a way to cooperate without simply giving in. If the child doesn't choose, the parent may need to take action, such as leaving the shop for now.
cards.apply_it: Before a predictable flashpoint, prepare two options you're happy with and offer the choice.

quiz.question: What makes a choice useful in the book's approach?
options: The child can pick anything they like
Both options are acceptable to the parent
quiz.explanation: When both choices are acceptable, the child gains some control while you keep the limit.

cards.title: Take action yourself, and let consequences teach
cards.body:
Sometimes words aren't enough. Faber and Mazlish suggest the parent can take action without punishing: if a child keeps running off in the shop, you leave; if a borrowed tool isn't returned, it isn't lent again for a while. The point is to protect yourself and others, not to inflict pain.

The book also suggests that, where it is safe, letting a child experience the natural result of their choice, such as a forgotten item, teaches more than a lecture.
cards.apply_it: Identify one situation where you can calmly take action instead of threatening, and decide what that action will be.

quiz.question: How is 'taking action' different from punishment in the book?
options: It is aimed at protection, not at making the child suffer
quiz.explanation: The action protects people or property; it isn't designed to hurt.

cards.title: Solve recurring problems together, step by step
cards.body:
For problems that keep coming back, Faber and Mazlish lay out a joint problem-solving method. First, talk about the child's feelings and needs. Then share your own, briefly. Next, brainstorm solutions together and write them all down without judging any. Finally, decide together which ideas you both can live with and how to follow through.

Children are far more committed to solutions they helped create, and they learn a skill they can use for life.
cards.apply_it: Choose one recurring battle and hold a short problem-solving session this week. Write every idea down, even silly ones.

quiz.question: What is the first step in the book's problem-solving method?
options: Talk about the child's feelings and needs
quiz.explanation: Starting with the child's side makes them more willing to hear yours.

cards.title: When brainstorming with a child, write down every idea first
cards.body:
A key part of the authors' problem-solving process is not judging ideas too soon. Every suggestion, however unrealistic, goes on the list. Evaluating comes later.

This matters because a child whose first idea is dismissed tends to stop contributing. Faber and Mazlish note that some odd suggestions turn out to contain something useful, and a light-hearted brainstorm can ease the tension around a long-running conflict.
cards.apply_it: In your next family discussion, appoint one person to write down every idea before anyone comments.

quiz.question: Why do the authors suggest writing down all ideas before judging them?
options: So children keep contributing and useful ideas aren't lost
Because all ideas will be used
To make the session last longer
quiz.explanation: Holding judgement keeps children engaged and lets good ideas surface.

cards.title: Let children make small choices every day
cards.body:
Faber and Mazlish argue that children become independent by practising decisions. Small, everyday choices, like which shirt to wear or whether to have half a glass of milk or a full one, give them practice in deciding and living with the result.

These moments build a child's sense that they have some control over their own life, which makes them less likely to fight for control in other ways.
cards.apply_it: Offer your child two small choices tomorrow, about clothes, food or order of tasks, and let them decide.

quiz.question: According to the book, what do small daily choices give children?
options: Practice in deciding and a sense of control
quiz.explanation: Small choices build decision-making skills and a sense of agency.

cards.title: Respect your child's struggle instead of rushing in
cards.body:
When a child is struggling with a jar lid or a hard homework problem, the book suggests acknowledging the difficulty rather than taking over or saying "it's easy". Telling a child something is easy makes them feel foolish if they fail, and takes the glory away if they succeed.

Faber and Mazlish suggest saying something like "jars can be tricky" and perhaps offering a tip, so the achievement remains theirs.
cards.apply_it: Next time your child struggles, say 'That's a tricky one' and wait before offering help.

quiz.question: Why do the authors advise against telling a struggling child 'it's easy'?
options: Because children should not try hard things
Because parents should do it instead
Because failing then feels shameful, and success feels small
quiz.explanation: Calling it easy raises the stakes of failing and shrinks the pride of succeeding.

cards.title: Ask fewer questions, and don't rush to answer theirs
cards.body:
Two quieter autonomy skills from the book. First, don't flood children with questions as soon as they come home; too many can feel like an invasion of privacy. Children often share more when they're not being interrogated.

Second, when a child asks you a question, resist answering immediately. Turning it back ("What do you think?") gives them a chance to think it through first. You can still help afterwards.
cards.apply_it: When your child next asks a question, reply with 'What do you think?' and listen to their answer before giving yours.

quiz.question: What do the authors suggest when a child asks a question?
options: Give them a chance to think about it first
Tell them to look it up
quiz.explanation: Pausing lets children practise thinking for themselves.

cards.title: Point children to help beyond home
cards.body:
Faber and Mazlish encourage parents to show children that they don't have to depend on their parents for everything. A librarian, a teacher, a coach, a dentist or an older cousin can all be sources of knowledge and help.

Learning to look outside the family for information builds a child's confidence and resourcefulness, and reduces the pressure on parents to be the answer to every question.
cards.apply_it: Next time your child asks something you'd normally answer, suggest a person or place outside the home who could help.

quiz.question: Why do the authors suggest pointing children to sources outside the home?
options: It builds their resourcefulness and independence
It keeps children out of the house
Outside sources are always more accurate
quiz.explanation: Using outside resources builds confidence and self-reliance.

cards.title: Don't take away a child's hope
cards.body:
When a child announces a big dream, it's tempting to prepare them for disappointment. Faber and Mazlish suggest holding back the warnings. A child who hopes to make the team or become an astronaut can explore that hope, learn from trying and find out for themselves.

Crushing a dream protects a child from nothing; it only takes away the motivation and learning that come from aiming high.
cards.apply_it: When your child shares a big ambition, ask a curious question about it instead of pointing out the obstacles.

quiz.question: What do the authors advise when a child shares a big, unlikely dream?
options: Let them keep the hope and explore it
Tell them about your own failures
quiz.explanation: Hope fuels effort and learning; warnings only remove it.

cards.title: Describe what you see instead of saying 'good job'
cards.body:
Faber and Mazlish argue that evaluative praise, like "good", "great" or "you're a genius", can make children uncomfortable, doubtful or anxious about keeping it up. Instead they recommend describing what you notice: "You put all the blocks back in the box, and sorted the red ones together."

Descriptive praise lets the child see their own achievement and draw their own conclusion about it, which builds self-esteem from the inside.
cards.apply_it: Next time you want to say 'good job', describe exactly what your child did instead.

quiz.question: What kind of praise do Faber and Mazlish recommend?
options: Describing specifically what the child did
quiz.explanation: Describing the effort lets children reach their own positive conclusion.

cards.title: Sum up their effort with one word that names a strength
cards.body:
After describing what a child did, the book suggests adding a single word that names the quality it showed: "That's what I call determination," or "That took patience."

Faber and Mazlish explain that this gives children a new piece of evidence about who they are, rooted in something they actually did. Unlike vague labels such as "good girl", a named strength is specific, believable and something to draw on next time.
cards.apply_it: Today, catch your child doing something well and name the strength it showed in one word.

quiz.question: What does summing up behaviour with one word do, according to the book?
options: Gives children a believable picture of a strength they have
quiz.explanation: A named strength grounded in real behaviour shapes a positive self-image.

cards.title: Free your child from labels like 'the lazy one' or 'the shy one'
cards.body:
Faber and Mazlish warn that children often live up, or down, to the roles adults give them. A child repeatedly called clumsy, shy or difficult may come to see that as who they are.

To free a child from a role, the authors suggest looking for moments that show them a different picture, putting them in situations where they can see themselves differently, and letting them overhear you say something positive about them.
cards.apply_it: Pick a label your child has picked up. This week, look for one moment that shows the opposite and point it out.

quiz.question: What risk do the authors see in labelling children?
options: Children may start to behave according to the label
quiz.explanation: Children tend to grow into the roles they're given.

cards.title: Be the keeper of your child's best moments
cards.body:
Another way the book suggests freeing a child from a negative role is to remind them of times they did better. Faber and Mazlish describe the parent as a storehouse of the child's special moments: "I remember when you stayed calm even though you lost the game."

When the child slips back into an old pattern, state your feelings or expectations plainly rather than repeating the label. And model the behaviour you hope to see.
cards.apply_it: Write down one moment this week when your child was at their best, so you can remind them of it later.

quiz.question: What do the authors mean by being a 'storehouse' for a child?
options: Remembering and reminding them of their best moments
quiz.explanation: Recalling past successes gives children evidence they can be different.
